For a possible input, choose the most frequent currently eligible letter. A max heap represents remaining counts, using negative counts for Python’s min-heap interface. The previously chosen letter must be temporarily ineligible: keep its remaining copies outside the heap for one turn. This enforces the adjacency rule without searching individual placements.

After choosing a different letter, reinsert the previously held letter if copies remain, then hold the newly chosen one. Spending the largest remaining counts early avoids leaving a dominant letter until the end. The result must include every original character, not merely form a valid prefix.

The reference checks for a remaining held count at termination as a final completeness guard. Any valid full rearrangement is accepted, so lexicographic tie choices in the heap do not constrain learner answers.

The majority bound is also sufficient for this schedule. Before a choice, let m be the total number of remaining copies. The held previous letter has at most floor(m/2) copies, because it cannot occupy the next slot; every other letter has at most ceil(m/2). Initially there is no held letter and the majority check establishes the second bound.

Select a largest available count and consume one copy. Its new held count fits floor((m-1)/2). If m is odd, at most one available letter can have ceil(m/2) copies; selecting the largest reduces that letter before the bound drops. If m is even, other letters may keep their counts because ceil((m-1)/2) is unchanged.

The old held count also fits the new available bound. Therefore the invariant continues. With copies still remaining, an empty heap would mean every copy belongs to the held letter, contradicting its at-most-half bound. Construction must finish.
